..(Saturday through Thursday)
Issued at 330 PM EST THU NOV 26 2026

While shortwave ridging is expected to briefly yield drier weather 
across Eastern Kentucky on Saturday, the progressive nature of the 
synoptic wave pattern aloft means that another storm system will 
traverse through the Greater Ohio River Valley on Sunday. This 
system is quite different than the one responsible for tonight's 
slushy snowfall though. Rather than a closed cold-core upper level 
low, this system will take the form of an sharp shortwave trough 
ejecting out of the Plains and into the upper midwest. The forecast 
area will be firmly positioned within the warm sector on the 
southeastern side of the troughing axis. The attendant, vertically-
stacked southwesterly jet streaks will advect ample moisture into 
the atmospheric column, which should yield a SW->NE increase in 
cloud cover on Saturday night. 

While confidence is high that Saturday will feature highs in the 50s 
amidst the clearer skies, it is uncertain how cold it will get on 
Saturday night and how warm it will get on Sunday afternoon. 
Northern and eastern valleys could decouple after sunset if 
overrunning moisture has not yet reached the CWA, with valley fog 
plausible given the recently wet grounds. The boundary layer should 
recouple as a robust low level jet (~60 knots at 850mb) spread 
across the area on Sunday morning. Expect the surface pressure 
gradient to tighten in this same time frame as a wave cyclone 
deepens upon approach. That low pressure system should track 
northeast along the Ohio River as the day progresses, yielding 
persistent southwesterly low level flow on Sunday afternoon. Winds 
could accordingly gust as high as 30mph on Sunday afternoon, with 
locally stronger gusts possible in the higher-elevation locales of 
SE KY, which are intrinsically closer to the core of those jet 
streaks aloft. Stronger wind gusts may also occur within any 
convective activity that develops ahead of the system's cold frontal 
passage on Sunday night. That convective development is not a 
guarantee though. 

The aforementioned AM cloud cover should linger through the 
afternoon hours and limit the amount of diurnal warming realized. 
Forecast highs will likely struggle to rise much higher than the 60 
degree mark, which leads to rather meager amounts of surface-based 
instability. There is a signal for some weak MUCAPE to emerge over 
Central Kentucky in this setup though. Likewise, the LREF resolves a 
mean of 30 knots of 0-3km bulk shear. For the 0-6km layer, those 
values jump to 60 knots. While this could be considered a [very] low 
cape, high-shear type setup, the cape-shear balance necessary for 
stronger storms is likely to be off kilter. With PWAT values above 
the 80th percentile of model climatology, such robust kinematics 
aloft though, and the presence of frontal forcing, a rumble of 
thunder cannot be entirely ruled out. The most likely forecast 
solution is another round of widespread rain showers, which will 
produce highly beneficial rainfall across the entire CWA. 
Nevertheless, it might be a good idea to secure any outdoor holiday 
decorations before Sunday's system arrives. The LREF/EPS ensemble 
resolves a 60-80% chance of non-thunderstorm winds in excess of 
30mph on Sunday. Winds of that magnitude will be sufficient to cause 
nuisance-level impacts, and wind headlines may need to be considered 
in future forecast packages (especially once this event enters the 
temporal range of the higher-resolution models/ensembles).

Zonal flow and surface high pressure looks to build into the CWA on 
Monday. This should yield seasonably dry and mild conditions for 
much of the upcoming work week. While ridge-valley splits are likely 
on Monday night, a weaker shortwave passing through the zonal flow 
regime could cause an increase in clouds on Tuesday night. That 
feature does not look deep enough to yield any meaningful low-level 
moisture return, but those clouds mean that Tuesday night will be 
warmer than Monday night. That warming continues through the end of 
the period, with highs moderating back into the 60s and lows 
approaching the 40 degree mark on Wednesday and Thursday. The 
attention then turns towards a system ejecting out of the Desert 
Southwest. That system is poised to bring about the area's next 
round of rain chances by Thursday night, but it is simply too early 
to discuss specific details that far out.
